title: Executable File Formats — Global Survey & Safety Assessment
author: MEARVK LLC — Galactic Cherry Marvell Edition 98
purpose: Assess all known executable formats for use, age, usefulness, structure, and safety.

formats.name: ELF
formats.status: Active — dominant on all Unix/Linux systems

structure.header: ELF header (52 or 64 bytes) identifies class (32/64), endianness, ABI, type
structure.segments: Program headers define loadable segments (LOAD, DYNAMIC, INTERP, NOTE)
structure.linking: Supports static and dynamic linking via PLT/GOT
structure.notes: Segment-based for execution, section-based for linking/debugging

assessment.safety_notes: No built-in code signing. Relies on OS-level protections (SELinux, ASLR, NX bit). LD_PRELOAD injection is trivial. Malware commonly distributed as ELF. Rootkits (Symbiote, BPFDoor, Reptile) all use ELF. Format itself is neutral — safety depends entirely on the OS enforcement layer.

formats.name: PE / PE32+
formats.magic: 0x4D 0x5A (MZ) — DOS stub, then PE\0\0 at offset in e_lfanew
formats.status: Active — dominant on all Windows systems

structure.dos_stub: Legacy MZ header (64 bytes) + DOS stub program
structure.pe_header: PE signature + COFF file header (machine, section count, timestamp)
structure.optional_header: Entry point, image base, section alignment, subsystem, DLL characteristics
structure.data_directories: Import table, export table, resource table, exception table, certificate table, debug, TLS, IAT, delay import
structure.overlay: Arbitrary data appended after last section (installers, packers abuse this)

assessment.safety_notes: Authenticode code signing exists but is optional. The most targeted executable format on Earth — vast majority of malware is PE. UAC and SmartScreen provide user-facing gates but are frequently bypassed. DLL side-loading and IAT hooking are systemic attack vectors. Overlay abuse for packed/encrypted payloads. Format complexity enables evasion techniques (section manipulation, header abuse, PE anomalies).

formats.name: Mach-O
formats.status: Active — sole native format for Apple platforms

structure.header: Mach header (magic, cpu type, cpu subtype, file type, load command count)
structure.load_commands: Ordered list: LC_SEGMENT_64, LC_DYLIB, LC_SYMTAB, LC_DYSYMTAB, LC_CODE_SIGNATURE, LC_ENCRYPTION_INFO
structure.fat_binary: Multi-architecture container (arm64 + x86_64 in one file)
structure.code_signature: Mandatory on iOS, enforced on macOS (notarization)

assessment.safety_notes: Apple enforces mandatory code signing on iOS and notarization on macOS. Gatekeeper prevents unsigned execution. Hardened runtime disables dangerous capabilities by default. DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES (the macOS LD_PRELOAD) is blocked for hardened binaries. The format itself includes LC_CODE_SIGNATURE as a first-class citizen. Strongest safety posture of the three major native formats due to Apple's walled-garden enforcement.

formats.name: a.out
formats.status: Obsolete — replaced by ELF in ~1995

structure.header: 32 bytes: magic, text size, data size, bss size, symbol table size, entry point, text reloc size, data reloc size
structure.limitations: No shared libraries (originally), no section flexibility, fixed layout

assessment.safety_notes: No security features whatsoever. No signing, no ASLR support, no dynamic linking guards. Purely historical. Any system still running a.out binaries is critically exposed. The simplicity is both its charm and its danger — there is nothing to enforce.

formats.name: COFF
platforms: Windows (as object format, basis of PE)
formats.status: Partially active — lives on as PE's internal object format and in embedded toolchains

structure.header: File header (machine, section count, timestamp, symbol pointer, flags)
structure.sections: Named sections with virtual/physical addresses, raw data pointer, relocations
structure.symbols: Symbol table with storage class and auxiliary entries
structure.notes: Predecessor to both PE and ELF. More structured than a.out but less flexible than ELF.

assessment.safety_notes: No signing, no runtime protections built into format. As an intermediate object format it is not directly executed by users, reducing attack surface. Its DNA lives on in PE where security was eventually bolted on.

formats.name: MZ (DOS EXE)
formats.status: Obsolete as standalone — survives as PE stub header

structure.header: 28-byte header: magic, last page bytes, page count, relocations, header size, min/max memory, initial SS:SP, checksum, initial CS:IP, relocation offset
structure.notes: Every PE file still begins with a valid MZ header for backward compatibility

assessment.safety_notes: No protections of any kind. Real-mode execution means full hardware access. No memory protection, no privilege separation, no signing. Only relevant today as the backward-compatible header in PE files or for retro computing.

formats.name: NE
formats.magic: NE after MZ stub (at offset e_lfanew)
formats.status: Obsolete

structure.header: NE header after MZ stub: module name, segment table, resource table, entry table
structure.segments: Named segments with attributes (moveable, preload, discardable)
structure.resources: Resource table for icons, dialogs, strings

assessment.safety_notes: 16-bit cooperative multitasking environment. No memory protection between processes. No code signing. Purely historical — any system running NE binaries in production is dangerously obsolete.

formats.name: COM
formats.status: Obsolete — historical curiosity

structure.body: Raw machine code, loaded verbatim at CS:0100h
structure.notes: The simplest possible executable format — pure code, no structure, no relocations

assessment.safety_notes: Absolute zero safety. No header means no validation possible — any 64KB blob of bytes is a valid COM file. No metadata, no signing, no structure to verify. Full real-mode hardware access. Trivial to craft malicious payloads. The only saving grace is the 64KB size limit constrains payload complexity.

formats.name: DEX
formats.status: Active — all Android applications

structure.header: Magic, checksum (Adler32), SHA-1 signature, file size, header size, endian tag
structure.sections: string_ids, type_ids, proto_ids, field_ids, method_ids, class_defs, data, map_list
structure.optimizations: ODEX (optimized DEX), VDEX, ART profiles for ahead-of-time compilation

formats.max_size: ~4 GB per DEX file (64K method limit per file, multidex for larger apps)

assessment.safety_notes: APK signing enforces integrity. Android 10+ supports embedded DEX execution directly from APK to prevent local tampering. Sandboxed execution within ART runtime with permission model. However, obfuscation techniques are common in malware. DEX can be trivially decompiled (jadx, apktool). Sideloading bypasses Play Protect. The format's safety depends heavily on the Play Store gate and device policy.

formats.name: Mach-O Fat / Universal Binary
formats.origin: NeXT (multi-architecture support), popularized by Apple for PowerPC→Intel→ARM transitions
formats.status: Active — used for arm64/x86_64 universal binaries

structure.fat_arch_entries: One per architecture: cpu type, cpu subtype, offset, size, alignment
structure.notes: The loader selects the appropriate slice at runtime

assessment.safety_notes: Inherits Mach-O security properties. Each slice is individually signed and notarized. The 0xCAFEBABE magic is shared with Java class files — this caused historical confusion in tooling but is not a security risk. Apple's code signing covers the entire fat binary.

formats.name: WebAssembly (Wasm)
formats.status: Active — rapidly growing, standardized by W3C

structure.sections: Ordered: Type, Import, Function, Table, Memory, Global, Export, Start, Element, Code, Data, DataCount
structure.encoding: Binary format with LEB128 integers, structured stack-based bytecode
structure.validation: Statically validated before execution — all types checked, all branches verified
structure.memory_model: Linear memory (resizable ArrayBuffer), no direct access to host memory

assessment.safety_notes: Security-by-design. Sandboxed execution with no direct access to host OS. Memory safety enforced by bounds-checked linear memory. No raw pointers to host. Static validation rejects malformed modules before execution. Cannot access filesystem, network, or hardware without explicit host imports. However: Wasm has been used for cryptomining malware (in-browser), and its opacity makes behavioral analysis harder than JavaScript. WASI extends capabilities but maintains capability-based security model.

formats.name: JAR
formats.status: Active — standard Java deployment format

structure.contents: Compiled .class files, resources, nested JARs, native libraries
structure.variants: WAR (web), EAR (enterprise), Spring Boot fat JAR

formats.max_size: Limited by ZIP format (~4 GB classic, ZIP64 for larger)

assessment.safety_notes: JVM provides sandboxed execution with bytecode verification. JAR signing is well-defined but rarely enforced in practice. Deserialization vulnerabilities (Log4Shell, etc.) are a systemic Java security concern. The ZIP-based format means JARs can be trivially inspected/modified. Classpath poisoning and dependency confusion attacks are real threats. SecurityManager was deprecated (Java 17) and removed, reducing in-process security boundaries.

formats.name: Shebang Script
formats.status: Active — universal mechanism for interpreter dispatch

structure.body: Plain text source code in the target language
structure.execution: Kernel reads shebang, exec()s the named interpreter with the script as argument
structure.notes: Not a true binary format — delegates to an interpreter. The script itself is just text.

assessment.safety_notes: Scripts are plaintext — trivially inspectable, which aids auditing. However: no signing mechanism built into the format. The shebang path can be manipulated (PATH hijacking). Scripts inherit the full privileges of the invoking user. Interpreter vulnerabilities (shell injection, eval abuse) are the primary attack vector. World-writable scripts are a classic privilege escalation target. No binary obfuscation means both easier auditing AND easier malicious modification.

formats.name: AppImage
formats.magic: ELF header (it's a self-extracting ELF with embedded filesystem)
formats.origin: Simon Peter (originally klik, then AppImage project)
formats.status: Active — popular for portable Linux apps

structure.filesystem: SquashFS image appended to the ELF
structure.contents: Application binary + all dependencies + desktop entry + icon
structure.execution: Runtime mounts SquashFS via FUSE, then exec()s the contained AppRun

assessment.safety_notes: No sandboxing whatsoever — the contained app runs with full user privileges. No mandatory signing (GPG is optional and rarely verified by users). Users download and chmod +x random files from the internet. No centralized update mechanism. No confinement, no permission model. Bundled libraries may contain known vulnerabilities that never get patched. The format trusts the user to trust the publisher.

formats.name: Snap
formats.status: Active — default on Ubuntu

structure.updates: Automatic delta updates, transactional (rollback on failure)

assessment.safety_notes: Mandatory store signing. AppArmor confinement in strict mode. Automatic security updates. However: 'classic' confinement (required by many dev tools) provides NO sandboxing. Snap Store has had incidents of malicious packages. The centralized store is a single point of trust/failure. snapd daemon runs as root.

formats.name: Flatpak
formats.status: Active — default on Fedora, available everywhere

structure.sandboxing: bubblewrap (user namespace) + seccomp + portals for controlled access
structure.runtimes: Shared base runtimes (freedesktop, GNOME, KDE) reduce duplication

assessment.safety_notes: Strongest sandboxing model of the three Linux universal formats. Portal-based permission system (file access, notifications, etc. gated by portals). Decentralized — anyone can host a Flatpak repo (Flathub is primary but not sole). Permissions are declared and reviewable. However: many apps request broad filesystem access which undermines the sandbox. Portal system adds complexity.

formats.name: XBE
formats.status: Obsolete — console discontinued 2009

structure.header: Magic, digital signature (256 bytes RSA), base address, header size, image size
structure.sections: Section headers with virtual address, size, flags (executable, writable, preload)
structure.certificates: Certificate area with title ID, title name, media types, game region, allowed media
structure.notes: PE-derived but simplified for console. Mandatory RSA signing (Microsoft private key).

formats.max_size: Limited by DVD disc size (~6 GB)

assessment.safety_notes: Mandatory RSA code signing — only Microsoft-signed XBEs run on retail hardware. The signing was eventually broken (softmod exploits), but the format itself enforces authentication. Closed platform means no user-facing execution of arbitrary code without exploit. Historical only.

formats.name: XEX
formats.status: Obsolete — console discontinued 2016

structure.header: Magic, module flags, PE data offset, security info offset
structure.security: RSA-2048 signature, SHA-256 content hashes, encrypted sections (AES-CBC)
structure.inner: Standard PE32 image (decrypted at load time by hypervisor)
structure.notes: Stronger than XBE — encryption + signing + hypervisor verification

assessment.safety_notes: Hardware-enforced security chain: eFuses → bootloader → hypervisor → XEX verification. Encrypted content with per-title keys. RSA-2048 + SHA-256. The hypervisor validates every page load. One of the most secure consumer executable formats ever deployed (took years to break). Historical only.

formats.name: AIF
formats.magic: ARM branch instruction at offset 0 (BL to entry)
formats.status: Obsolete — replaced by ELF on modern ARM

structure.header: 128 bytes: decompress code, self-reloc code, zero-init code, image entry, RO size, RW size, debug size, ZI size, debug type, image base, workspace
structure.notes: Simple format for bare-metal ARM. The header itself is executable ARM code.

assessment.safety_notes: No signing, no protections. Bare-metal format for embedded ARM — security is not its concern. The header being executable code is novel but means the first 128 bytes are also attack surface.

formats.name: Flat Binary
formats.status: Active — ubiquitous in firmware and embedded

structure.body: Raw bytes — could be code, data, or both
structure.loading: Loaded at a fixed address known by convention (e.g., 0x7C00 for BIOS boot sector)
structure.notes: The loader must know the load address, entry point, and size externally

assessment.safety_notes: No structure means no validation, no signing (unless externally applied), no metadata. Used for boot sectors, firmware blobs, and FPGA bitstreams. UEFI Secure Boot adds external signing to firmware images. Without external protection, a flat binary is completely unverifiable. Critical that surrounding infrastructure provides authentication.

formats.name: PE/COFF for UEFI
platforms: All UEFI firmware (x86, x86-64, ARM, RISC-V)
formats.status: Active — boots every modern PC

structure.format: Subset of PE32+ with EFI subsystem type
structure.entry: EFI_MAIN entry point receives SystemTable and ImageHandle
structure.notes: Runs in firmware context — ring 0 equivalent, before OS loads

formats.max_size: Limited by firmware memory (typically 256 MB EFI partition)

assessment.safety_notes: UEFI Secure Boot enforces code signing (Microsoft + vendor keys in db). Bootkits like Bootkitty (2024, first Linux UEFI bootkit) demonstrate that the pre-OS environment is a high-value target. If Secure Boot is bypassed or disabled, EFI binaries run with absolute hardware access. The format itself supports signing via the PE certificate table. Safety is strong WHEN Secure Boot is properly configured and key management is sound.

formats.name: DMG (Apple Disk Image)
formats.magic: 0x78 0x01 (zlib), or 'koly' trailer at end of file
formats.status: Active — standard macOS application distribution format

structure.format: UDIF (Universal Disk Image Format) — a disk image, not an executable
structure.filesystem: Contains HFS+ or APFS filesystem with .app bundle
structure.signing: Code signing on the contained .app bundle (Mach-O inside)
structure.notes: DMG is a container/distribution format, not an executable format itself. The executable is the Mach-O inside the .app inside the filesystem inside the DMG.

assessment.safety_notes: The DMG itself can be signed and notarized by Apple. Gatekeeper checks the DMG and its contents. However: DMGs are routinely used to distribute macOS malware (user mounts, drags to Applications). The 'mount and drag' workflow bypasses fine-grained permission checks. Notarization requirement (macOS Catalina+) significantly improved safety for apps distributed outside the App Store.

formats.name: MSI
formats.status: Active — standard Windows installation format

structure.database: Relational database of installation tables (Component, File, Registry, CustomAction)
structure.custom_actions: Arbitrary code execution during install (DLLs, scripts, EXEs)
structure.signing: Authenticode signature on the MSI file

assessment.safety_notes: CustomActions are arbitrary code that runs during installation — often with elevated privileges. MSI repair/reinstall can be triggered silently. The format's complexity enables abuse (DLL side-loading via CustomAction, privilege escalation via repair). Authenticode signing helps but is not mandatory. Enterprise deployment (GPO) trusts MSIs broadly. MSI transform files (.mst) can silently alter installation behavior.

formats.name: MSIX / AppX
formats.status: Active — Microsoft's recommended packaging format

assessment.safety_notes: Mandatory signing — unsigned MSIX cannot be installed. Declared capabilities restrict access (no silent filesystem access). Container isolation. Clean install/uninstall with no registry pollution. The strongest safety model in the Windows ecosystem. However: limited adoption for legacy Win32 apps, and the 'runFullTrust' capability effectively disables sandboxing for packaged desktop apps.

formats.name: ELF Core Dump
formats.status: Active — standard crash dump format

structure.segments: PT_NOTE (process state, registers, signal info) + PT_LOAD (memory pages)
structure.contents: Complete process memory state at time of crash/signal
structure.notes: Not executable — contains the frozen state of a crashed process for post-mortem debugging

formats.max_size: Can be enormous (GBs for large processes)

assessment.safety_notes: Core dumps contain EVERYTHING that was in process memory at crash time — passwords, encryption keys, tokens, session data, private keys. A core dump is a security-sensitive artifact that should never be world-readable. Systems should limit core dump generation (ulimit -c 0) in production. The format itself is passive (not executable) but the data it contains is extremely sensitive.

safest_formats.name: MSIX/AppX
safest_formats.reason: Mandatory signing, declared capabilities, container isolation

safest_formats.name: Mach-O
safest_formats.reason: Mandatory code signing (iOS), notarization (macOS), hardened runtime

most_useful_today.reason: Runs the internet (Linux servers), Android, embedded

observations.evolutionary_pattern: a.out (1971) → COFF (1983) → ELF (1983/adopted 1995). MZ (1981) → NE (1985) → PE (1993). Each generation adds metadata, relocations, and eventually signing.
observations.safety_trend: Modern formats (Wasm, MSIX, Flatpak) design security in from day one. Legacy formats (ELF, PE, Mach-O) bolt security on via OS enforcement. The oldest formats (COM, a.out, MZ) have zero security by design.
observations.convergence: ELF, PE, and Mach-O have converged on similar feature sets: sections, symbols, relocations, dynamic linking, position independence. The differences are structural/historical rather than capability-based.
observations.container_vs_executable: Modern trend separates the container (signing, metadata, sandboxing) from the executable (native code). Flatpak, Snap, AppImage, MSIX, DMG are all containers around native binaries. This layered approach allows security policy without changing the binary format.
observations.the_signing_gap: ELF — the format running most of the internet's infrastructure — has NO built-in code signing. Linux relies entirely on OS-level mechanisms (dm-verity, IMA/EVM, package manager GPG). This is the single largest structural security gap in modern computing.

relevance_to_galactic_cherry.kernel_native: ELF — all kernel modules (.ko), userspace, shared libraries

relevance_to_galactic_cherry.negamane_protects: All format binaries equally — filesystem-level immutability
